opener.label: Before any circle theorems

steps.pre: The spoke meets the road at
steps.say: A puzzle about a bicycle wheel. No circle theorems needed yet, just picture it.
steps.hint: The spoke points straight down and the road is flat and level.

steps.pre: The angle between the stick and the downward spoke is
steps.say: The road only touches the wheel at that one point, so it is a tangent. The spoke is a radius. A tangent and a radius always meet at 90°. That is one of the seven circle theorems you will use today. Now a straight stick leans against the tyre at that same point, rising at 25° from the ground.
steps.hint: The stick splits the right angle: 90 − 25.

steps.say: You just used a right angle as a stepping stone, splitting 90° into two parts. That is exactly the move the harder questions need: find one angle, then use it to reach the next.

steps: Identify the circle parts: centre, radius, tangent, chord, arc, segment
Solve and state the theorem as your reason
method_card.title: Circle Theorems
method_card.content:
Key theorems:

1. Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference (from the same arc).

2. Angle in a semicircle is \(90°\).

3. Angles in the same segment are equal.

4. Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to \(180°\).

5. A tangent meets the radius at \(90°\).

6. Tangents from an external point are equal in length.

7. Alternate segment: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
method_card.example:
The angle at the centre is \(140°\). Find the angle at the circumference.

Angle at circumference = \(140 ÷ 2 = 70°\) (angle at centre is twice angle at circumference).

steps: Gold questions need two or more facts in a row. Find every angle you can from one theorem, then feed it into the next.
A diameter gives a 90° angle in the semicircle; two radii make an isosceles triangle; a tangent meets a radius at 90° so Pythagoras can find a length.
Finish by checking your angles add to 180° in a triangle, or 360° in a quadrilateral.
gold.title: Gold: chain theorems together

steps.label: Isosceles
steps.content: OB = OC (radii), so the base angles are equal: \((180 − 80) ÷ 2 = 50°\).

example.question: A, B, C lie on a circle, centre O. Angle BAC = 40° at the circumference. Find the base angle of isosceles triangle OBC.

steps: Spot which single circle theorem the diagram is about: angle at the centre, angle in a semicircle, same segment, cyclic quadrilateral, or tangent meeting a radius.
Write the fact as a sum or a halving or doubling, then read off the answer.
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference; opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°.
bronze.title: Bronze: one theorem, one step

steps.label: Theorem
steps.content: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so halve it.

example.question: Angle at the centre is 100°. Find the angle at the circumference.

steps: Apply the theorem, then make a second move: take a reflex angle (360° minus the centre angle), add up a triangle's angles, or form an equation.
For a reflex angle at the centre, subtract from 360° before halving to the circumference.
When angles are given as expressions like \(3x + 5\), set the opposite pair equal to 180°, then solve for x.
silver.title: Silver: two steps, or an equation

example.question: Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles are \(2x\) and \(x + 30\). Find x.

gold.hint: Alternate segment theorem: the tangent-chord angle equals the angle the chord subtends in the alternate segment.
gold.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA chord AB subtends \(40°\) at the circumference. A tangent at A makes angle \(x°\) with the chord AB. Find \(x\).

guided_steps.say: The alternate segment theorem: the tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment. The chord AB subtends 40° at the circumference, which is that alternate angle.

guided_steps.pre: Write the angle in the alternate segment:
guided_steps.hint: The angle the chord subtends at the circumference.

guided_steps.pre: By the theorem, x equals it: x =
guided_steps.hint: The tangent-chord angle equals the alternate angle.

guided_steps.pre: Both angles stand on chord AB and are equal, so their sum is 40 + 40 =
guided_steps.done: Two equal 40° angles, so x = 40° is right.

misconceptions.message: By the alternate segment theorem the tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment, so x = 40°. Doing 180 − 40 = 140° treats them as supplementary, which is wrong.

gold.hint: Double to the centre, take the reflex (360 minus it), then halve.
gold.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyAngle at circumference from the minor arc = \(28°\). Find the angle at circumference from the major arc.

guided_steps.say: Work through the centre. The minor-arc angle at the circumference is 28°, so the centre angle on the minor arc is twice that.

guided_steps.pre: Major-arc circumference angle = half the reflex: 304 ÷ 2 =

guided_steps.done: They total 180°, opposite angles on the two arcs, so 152° is right.

misconceptions.message: The two angles stand on opposite arcs, so they are supplementary, not equal. Centre (minor) = 56°, reflex = 304°, half = 152°. Answering 28° treats them as angles in the same segment.

gold.hint: The tangent meets the radius at 90°; use Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle.
gold.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyFrom P outside a circle, tangent PA has length 12 and line PB passes through centre O, with PO = 13. Find the radius.

guided_steps.say: PA is a tangent, so it meets the radius OA at 90°. Triangle OAP is right-angled at A, with radius OA and tangent PA as the short sides and PO as the hypotenuse.

guided_steps.done: That equals 13², so the radius is 5.

misconceptions.message: PA is a tangent, so it meets radius OA at 90°. Use Pythagoras: r² + 12² = 13², so r² = 169 − 144 = 25 and r = 5. Simply subtracting 13 − 12 = 1 skips Pythagoras.

gold.hint: Angles A and C are opposite, so add them and set the total equal to 180°.
gold.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyIn a cyclic quadrilateral, angle A = \(2x + 10\), angle B = \(3y\), angle C = \(x + 20\), angle D = \(2y + 30\). Find \(x\).

guided_steps.say: Angles A and C are opposite, so they add to 180°: \((2x + 10) + (x + 20) = 180\). (B and D are the other pair.)

guided_steps.pre: Add the x-terms of A and C: 2x + x =

guided_steps.done: Angle C = 50 + 20 = 70, and 110 + 70 = 180, so x = 50 is right.

misconceptions.message: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°, not 360°: 3x + 30 = 180 gives x = 50. Using 360 gives 3x + 30 = 360, so x = 110.

gold.hint: The diameter gives a 90° angle at B; find angle BCA, then use angles in the same segment on chord AB.
gold.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA, B, C and D are points on a circle. AC is a diameter and angle BAC = \(34°\). B and D lie on opposite sides of the diameter AC. Find angle ADB.

guided_steps.say: AC is a diameter, so the angle in the semicircle at B is 90°: angle ABC = 90°.

guided_steps.pre: The angle in the semicircle, angle ABC, is
guided_steps.hint: Angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

guided_steps.pre: Triangle ABC angle sum: angle BCA = 180 − 90 − 34 =

guided_steps.say: Angle ADB and angle BCA both stand on chord AB, and C and D are on the same arc, so they are angles in the same segment: equal.

guided_steps.hint: Equal to the angle you just found.

guided_steps.done: The triangle totals 180°, and angle ADB equals angle BCA in the same segment, so angle ADB = 56°.

misconceptions.message: Angle BCA = 56° from the semicircle right angle and the triangle's angle sum. Since C and D lie on the same arc, angle ADB = angle BCA = 56°. Treating them as supplementary gives 180 − 56 = 124°, which only applies to points on opposite arcs.

bronze.hint: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so halve it.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyAngle at centre = \(120°\). Find the angle at the circumference.

guided_steps.say: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc, so the circumference angle is half the centre angle.

guided_steps.pre: The centre angle is how many times the circumference angle?
guided_steps.hint: The centre angle is twice as big.

guided_steps.done: That returns the centre angle of 120°, so 60° is right.
guided_steps.hint: Double your answer; it should give the centre angle.

misconceptions.message: The centre angle is twice the circumference angle, so you halve to go from centre to edge: 120 ÷ 2 = 60°. Doubling instead gives 240°, bigger than a full turn.

bronze.hint: The centre angle is twice the circumference angle, so double it.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyAngle at circumference = \(35°\). Find the angle at the centre.

guided_steps.say: Going the other way, the centre angle is twice the circumference angle, so double it.

guided_steps.pre: The centre angle is how many times the circumference angle?

guided_steps.done: That returns the circumference angle of 35°, so 70° is right.
guided_steps.hint: Halve your answer; it should give the circumference angle.

misconceptions.message: From the edge to the centre you double, not halve: 35 × 2 = 70°. Halving gives 17.5°, smaller than the edge angle, so it cannot be the bigger centre angle.

bronze.hint: The angle in a semicircle is always a right angle.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA triangle is drawn in a semicircle with the diameter as one side. What is the angle opposite the diameter?

guided_steps.say: The diameter passes through the centre, so it makes a straight angle at the centre.

guided_steps.pre: The straight angle across the diameter, at the centre, is
The angle at the circumference is half the centre angle: 180 ÷ 2 =
So the other two angles of the triangle add up to 180 − 90 =
guided_steps.done: The right angle plus the other two (90°) totals 180°, the triangle's angle sum, so the angle opposite the diameter is 90°.

misconceptions.message: The diameter subtends 180° at the centre, and the angle at the circumference is half of that: 180 ÷ 2 = 90°. Using 180° forgets to halve.

bronze.hint: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyCyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles are \(85°\) and \(x°\). Find \(x\).

guided_steps.say: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.

guided_steps.pre: The two opposite angles must total

guided_steps.done: They total 180°, so x = 95° is right.

misconceptions.message: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, not equal: x = 180 − 85 = 95°. Answering 85° treats them as equal, which is the same-segment rule, not the cyclic-quad rule.

bronze.hint: The tangent meets the radius at 90°; the three angles of the triangle add to 180°.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyOT is a radius and TP is a tangent touching the circle at T. In triangle OTP, the angle at P is \(35°\). Find angle TOP (the angle at O).

guided_steps.say: A tangent meets a radius at 90°, so the angle at T, angle OTP, is a right angle.

guided_steps.pre: The angle at T (radius meets tangent) is
guided_steps.hint: Tangent meets radius at a right angle.

guided_steps.pre: The three angles add to 180°, so angle TOP = 180 − 90 − 35 =
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the right angle and the 35° from 180.

guided_steps.done: They total 180°, the triangle's angle sum, so angle TOP = 55° is right.

misconceptions.message: The tangent meets the radius at 90°, so the triangle already has a right angle. Angle TOP = 180 − 90 − 35 = 55°. Forgetting the right angle and doing 180 − 35 gives 145°.

bronze.hint: Angles in the same segment are equal, so x matches the 42°.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyTwo angles are in the same segment. One is \(42°\), the other is \(x°\). Find \(x\).

guided_steps.say: Angles in the same segment stand on the same chord and are equal.

guided_steps.pre: Equal angles, so the difference between them is
So x equals the given angle: x =

guided_steps.done: Zero difference confirms they are equal, so x = 42°.
guided_steps.hint: Equal angles should differ by zero.

misconceptions.message: You may have confused this with the cyclic quadrilateral rule. Angles in the same segment are EQUAL, not supplementary, so x = 42°, not 180 − 42 = 138°.

bronze.hint: The centre angle is twice the circumference angle, so halve it.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyAngle at centre = \(160°\). Find the angle at the circumference.

guided_steps.say: The centre angle is twice the circumference angle, so halve it.

guided_steps.pre: The centre angle is how many times the circumference angle?

guided_steps.done: That returns the centre angle of 160°, so 80° is right.
guided_steps.hint: Double your answer; it should give the centre angle.

misconceptions.message: Halve to go from centre to edge: 160 ÷ 2 = 80°. Doubling gives 320°, more than a full turn, so it cannot be an angle at the edge.

bronze.hint: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyCyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles are \(x°\) and \(105°\). Find \(x\).

guided_steps.say: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.

guided_steps.pre: The two opposite angles must total

guided_steps.done: They total 180°, so x = 75° is right.

misconceptions.message: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: x = 180 − 105 = 75°. Answering 105° treats them as equal, which is wrong for a cyclic quadrilateral.

silver.hint: Double the circumference angle for the centre angle, then subtract from 360° for the reflex.
silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyThe angle at the circumference is \(54°\). Find the reflex angle at the centre standing on the same arc.

guided_steps.say: First the ordinary angle at the centre is twice the circumference angle.

guided_steps.pre: The reflex angle is the rest of the full turn: 360 − 108 =

guided_steps.done: The two centre angles complete 360°, so the reflex angle is 252°.
guided_steps.hint: The two centre angles should complete a full turn.

misconceptions.message: You found the ordinary centre angle, 2 × 54 = 108°, but the question asks for the reflex angle: 360 − 108 = 252°.

silver.hint: Alternate segment theorem: the tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment.
silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA tangent and a chord meet at a point on the circle. The angle in the alternate segment is \(63°\). Find the angle between the tangent and the chord.

guided_steps.say: The alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.

guided_steps.pre: Write the angle in the alternate segment:
By the theorem the tangent-chord angle equals it, so it is
guided_steps.hint: The tangent-chord angle equals the alternate angle.

guided_steps.pre: Two equal angles: their sum is 63 + 63 =
guided_steps.done: Two equal 63° angles sum to 126°, confirming the tangent-chord angle is 63°.

misconceptions.message: The alternate segment theorem makes them equal, not supplementary: the angle is 63°. Doing 180 − 63 = 117° wrongly treats them as adding to 180°.

silver.hint: Opposite angles sum to 180°. Add the two expressions and set the total equal to 180.
silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyIn a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = \(3x + 5\) and angle C = \(2x + 15\). Find \(x\).

guided_steps.say: A and C are opposite angles, so they add to 180°: \((3x + 5) + (2x + 15) = 180\).

guided_steps.done: Angle C = 2 × 32 + 15 = 79, and 101 + 79 = 180, so x = 32 is right.

misconceptions.message: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°, not 360°: 5x + 20 = 180 gives x = 32. Using 360 gives 5x + 20 = 360, so x = 68.

silver.hint: The radius meets the tangent at 90°; the chord splits that right angle.
silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyAT is a tangent to a circle with centre O, touching at A. AB is a chord. The angle between the tangent and the chord, angle TAB, is \(55°\). Find angle OAB.

guided_steps.say: OA is a radius and AT is a tangent, so they meet at 90°: angle OAT = 90°.

guided_steps.pre: The right angle between radius and tangent is
guided_steps.hint: Tangent meets radius at a right angle.

guided_steps.pre: The chord AB splits that right angle, so angle OAB = 90 − 55 =

guided_steps.done: The two parts rebuild the 90° right angle, so angle OAB = 35° is right.
guided_steps.hint: The two parts should rebuild the right angle.

misconceptions.message: The radius and tangent meet at 90°, and the chord splits that into angle OAB and the 55° angle. So angle OAB = 90 − 55 = 35°. Answering 55° gives the tangent-chord angle instead.

silver.hint: Tangents drawn from an external point are equal in length.
silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyFrom point P outside a circle, two tangents PA and PB are drawn. PA = 8 cm. Find PB.

guided_steps.say: Two tangents drawn from the same external point are equal in length.

guided_steps.done: Two equal 8 cm tangents total 16 cm, so PB = 8 cm.

misconceptions.message: Tangents from the same external point are equal, so PB = PA = 8 cm.

silver.hint: Use the reflex angle at the centre (360 − 110), then halve it.
silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyAngle at centre (minor arc) = \(110°\). Find the angle at the circumference from the major arc.

guided_steps.say: The 110° at the centre is on the minor-arc side. The major-arc circumference angle stands on the reflex angle at the centre.

guided_steps.pre: Angle at the circumference is half the reflex: 250 ÷ 2 =

guided_steps.done: Doubling returns the reflex centre angle of 250°, so 125° is right.
guided_steps.hint: Double your answer; it should give the reflex angle.

misconceptions.message: The major-arc angle stands on the reflex centre angle. Reflex = 360 − 110 = 250°, then halve: 250 ÷ 2 = 125°. Halving the 110° directly gives 55°, the wrong centre angle.

silver.hint: The angle in the semicircle is 90°; the three angles of the triangle sum to 180°.
silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA triangle inscribed in a semicircle has one angle of \(90°\) (at the circumference) and another of \(32°\). Find the third angle.

guided_steps.say: The 90° is the angle in the semicircle. The three angles of the triangle add to 180°.

guided_steps.done: They total 180°, the triangle's angle sum, so the third angle is 58°.

misconceptions.message: All three angles of the triangle add to 180°: third = 180 − 90 − 32 = 58°. Forgetting the 90° and doing 180 − 32 gives 148°.

problem_bank.gold_description: Chain two or more theorems, or bring in Pythagoras, to reach the answer.
problem_bank.bronze_description: Recall and apply one circle theorem in a single step.
problem_bank.silver_description: Combine a theorem with a second step: a reflex angle, an angle sum, or a short equation.
